passage:
Kalyani, you asked why I let the team choose the release date. I'm Arnab, and I learned it the hard way. In my first month as a lead I felt a rush: people waited for my nod. I started checking every line of code and rewriting slides in meetings so everyone could see how sharp I was.

One evening the quietest engineer, Praveen, said, "You've redone my work twice. Should I stop trying?" That sentence stuck like a splinter. I went home ashamed.

The next morning I handed Praveen the whole module and stepped back. Within a week the team was fixing problems before they reached me. I understood then that my job was helping them succeed. Power that feeds my ego had been costing me the team.

qa.q: What did Praveen say to Arnab?
qa.a: Praveen said, 'You've redone my work twice. Should I stop trying?'

qa.q: What did Arnab feel in the first month as a lead?
qa.a: A rush of excitement from people waiting for Arnab's nod, which pushed Arnab to check everything and show off.

qa.q: What did Arnab change after Praveen's words?
qa.a: Arnab handed over the whole module and stepped back, seeing the job as helping the team succeed.

qa.q: How might Praveen have felt after being redone twice?
qa.a: Discouraged, enough to ask whether to stop trying.

grounding: A new lead enjoys the rush of authority and starts micromanaging, notices it, delegates and treats the job as helping others succeed.

passage:
You asked what surprised me about becoming a manager. I'm Vishal, and honestly? How much I liked the power. That's embarrassing to say out loud.

The first month, I checked every commit Baljeet made. Every one. I rewrote his emails before they went to the client. In meetings I'd explain things he already knew, loudly, so the director would hear. It felt good. It felt like I mattered.

Then one evening Baljeet said, very politely, "Vishal bhai, should I just stop writing code and send you my ideas instead?" He was smiling. His eyes weren't.

That night I couldn't sleep. I realised I was using the team to feel big.

So I changed a few things. I gave Baljeet the client module, fully. I stopped reviewing everything and agreed one check-in a week. And I started asking, at the end of each meeting, "What's blocking you, and how can I help?"

He delivered it early. That felt better than any rush.

qa.q: What did Baljeet ask Vishal one evening?
qa.a: He asked, "Vishal bhai, should I just stop writing code and send you my ideas instead?"

qa.q: How did Vishal feel when he enjoyed checking everything?
qa.a: Vishal felt a rush of power and importance, which later turned to embarrassment.

qa.q: What changes helped Vishal lead better?
qa.a: He handed Baljeet the client module fully, cut reviews to one weekly check-in, and asked what was blocking people and how he could help.

qa.q: How did Baljeet feel about being micromanaged?
qa.a: Baljeet felt frustrated and belittled, which showed in his polite but pointed question and unsmiling eyes.

grounding: A spoken account shows a young manager who enjoys the rush of authority and starts micromanaging, notices it, delegates, and sees his job as helping others succeed.

passage:
Week one. Anjali had waited three years to lead the design team. On Monday she moved her desk to the centre of the room. She asked for hourly updates. When Binita presented a layout, Anjali redrew it in front of the client "to show how it's done". Driving home, she felt powerful and oddly restless.

Week three, a Wednesday. Binita didn't come in. She'd emailed HR asking to move teams. Anjali read the email twice, her face burning. She asked her own manager, Mr. Rao, what she was doing wrong. He said gently, "You're making them smaller so you feel bigger."

Week six, a Friday. Anjali had cancelled the hourly updates. She had given Binita the full festive campaign and stayed out of it except for a Tuesday review. At the client meeting she said, "This is Binita's concept," and stepped back. Binita stayed on the team.

qa.q: What did Binita email HR about?
How did Anjali feel reading Binita's email to HR?
qa.a: Anjali felt ashamed, her face burning, realising something was wrong with how she was leading.

qa.q: What did Anjali change by week six?
qa.a: She stopped hourly updates, delegated the full campaign to Binita, and credited her to the client, focusing on helping her succeed.

qa.q: How did Binita experience Anjali's first weeks as lead?
qa.a: Binita felt belittled and undermined, especially when her layout was redrawn in front of the client.

grounding: The story shows a new manager who enjoys authority and micromanages until the team suffers, then notices it, delegates and sees her job as helping others succeed.
